name: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome
populations: athletes in running and jumping sports
summary: Reproducible exertional leg pain and tightness from raised compartment pressure, settling quickly with rest. The anterior compartment is most often involved. Treatment is gait retraining or fasciotomy.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: No reliable timeline. A 6-week running-style program gave gains in small series; fasciotomy helped about two-thirds of young athletes

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Symptom-guided graded running after gait retraining; after fasciotomy, per the surgeon's protocol and symptom response

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Dynamic intracompartmental pressure testing, though the pressure criteria overlap the range in healthy people

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Exercise MRI, near-infrared spectroscopy and pressure testing have similar sensitivity; imaging also excludes other causes

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: 15–25 years in one review; mean age 26.6 in a surgical systematic review

keyFacts.label: Compartments
keyFacts.value: Anterior 51%, lateral 33%, deep posterior 13%, superficial posterior 3% in surgical series

overview:
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS) is exercise-related leg pain, tightness and sometimes weakness or paraesthesia that builds at a reproducible point in exercise and settles quickly after stopping. It is thought to result from an exercise-related rise in pressure within one or more fascial compartments, which compromises circulation and muscle function [r1,r2]. It mainly affects young, physically active people aged 15–25 and is under-diagnosed [r2].

The cause is not fully understood [r3]. The pressure criteria used for diagnosis overlap the range found in healthy people, which challenges both the diagnostic thresholds and the underlying pathophysiology [r4]. In surgical series the anterior compartment was most often involved (51%), then the lateral (33%), the deep posterior (13%) and the superficial posterior (3%) compartment [r5]. Conservative options include activity modification, gait retraining and botulinum toxin injections, and fasciotomy is used for persistent symptoms [r3,r2]. Outcomes after surgery are good in many but not all athletes: about two-thirds of young athletic patients had a successful result in a systematic review [r5], and in a large military cohort nearly half reported symptom recurrence [r6].

epidemiology.text: A systematic review of 24 surgical studies (1,596 patients) found a mean age of 26.6 years, with 70% male patients; the groups were mostly military personnel (54%) and athletes (29%), of whom 83% were recreational. The anterior compartment was involved in 51%, the lateral in 33%, the deep posterior in 13% and the superficial posterior in 3% [r5]. In a cohort of 611 military patients who had fasciotomy, the average age was 28.0 years and 91.8% were male [r6]. A recent review describes CECS as under-diagnosed, affecting people aged 15–25, and typically bilateral [r2]. The male predominance in surgical series probably reflects the military populations studied, and true population incidence has not been well defined in the sources reviewed.

intrinsic: Male sex in surgical and military series (70% and 91.8%), although these samples are skewed toward military populations [r5,r6]
Bilateral involvement is typical, which may reflect shared anatomical or mechanical factors [r2]
Muscle herniae through the fascia on examination (45.9% of patients with CECS versus 12.9% of those without in a retrospective study) [r7]
extrinsic: Running and other repetitive high-impact exercise: CECS occurs almost exclusively with running [r1]
Military training and marching, where large numbers of cases are reported [r5]
Heel-strike running mechanics (modifiable): a shift to forefoot running lowered intracompartmental pressure in small series, which suggests mechanics contribute [r1,r8]

mechanism.summary: CECS develops over weeks of repeated exercise rather than from a single injury. During exercise, intramuscular pressure rises within a compartment bounded by bone, interosseous membrane and deep fascia. The rise compromises circulation, limits muscle function and causes pain [r1]. The precise cause is unknown, and the commonly used pressure criteria do not clearly separate patients from healthy people [r3,r4]. Symptoms subside quickly after stopping [r2].
sequence: The athlete starts a run or march at normal pace; the leg muscles work with each stride and the foot strike repeatedly loads the lower leg.
Muscle blood flow and volume rise during sustained exertion inside a closed fascial compartment that cannot expand much.
Intramuscular pressure climbs and stays high; pressure after exercise is the basis of the commonly used diagnostic criteria [r7].
Raised pressure compromises circulation and muscle function [r1].
Tightness, pain, cramping, weakness and sometimes paraesthesia develop at a reproducible time or distance into exercise [r3].
The athlete stops, pressure falls and symptoms subside quickly [r2].
The same pattern repeats in the next session until the mechanics, load or compartment are changed.

variants.name: Anterior compartment CECS (most common)
variants.description: Tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus; involved in 51% of surgical cases. The deep peroneal nerve runs within the compartment, so numbness in the first web space and weak dorsiflexion can occur [r5,r3].

variants.name: Lateral compartment CECS
variants.description: Peroneal muscles; involved in 33% of surgical cases and often together with the anterior compartment [r5].

variants.name: Deep posterior compartment CECS
variants.description: Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus; involved in 13% of surgical cases. Its symptoms overlap with medial tibial stress syndrome and are difficult to separate clinically [r5,r9].

variants.name: Superficial posterior compartment CECS
variants.description: Gastrocnemius and soleus; the least common (3% of surgical cases) [r5].

anatomy.text: The lower leg has four fascial compartments bounded by the tibia, fibula, interosseous membrane and deep crural fascia. The anterior compartment contains tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, the anterior tibial artery and the deep peroneal nerve. The lateral compartment contains peroneus longus and brevis with the superficial peroneal nerve. The superficial posterior compartment contains gastrocnemius and soleus, and the deep posterior compartment contains tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus with the posterior tibial neurovascular bundle. Surgical series show the anterior compartment is involved most often, followed by the lateral compartment [r5].

structures.name: Anterior compartment
structures.role: Ankle and toe dorsiflexors; the compartment most often affected in CECS (51% of surgical cases) [r5]

structures.name: Lateral compartment
structures.role: Evertors of the foot (peroneals); involved in about one-third of surgical cases [r5]

structures.name: Deep posterior compartment
structures.role: Foot inverters and toe flexors; symptoms overlap with medial tibial stress syndrome [r9]

structures.name: Superficial posterior compartment
structures.role: Gastrocnemius and soleus, the main plantarflexors; least often affected [r5]

structures.name: Deep crural fascia
structures.role: Fibrous sleeve that limits compartment expansion; fascial defects through which muscle herniates are more common in CECS [r7]

structures.name: Deep peroneal nerve and anterior tibial artery
structures.role: Run within the anterior compartment, so raised pressure can cause paraesthesia and weakness [r3]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The accepted model is that exercise raises pressure within a compartment and that this pressure compromises circulation and muscle function, which causes pain [r1]. Pedowitz and colleagues proposed diagnostic criteria based on intramuscular pressures recorded before and after exercise: a pre-exercise pressure of 15 mmHg or more, a 1-minute post-exercise pressure of 30 mmHg or more, or a 5-minute post-exercise pressure of 20 mmHg or more [r7]. A systematic review of 38 studies found that, except for relaxation pressure, these criteria overlap the ranges recorded in healthy subjects, and several studies reported mean pressures that would be called positive in people with no symptoms [r4].

The pathophysiology is therefore poorly understood [r4,r3]. In a prospective study of 50 patients, intracompartmental pressure at a 35 mmHg cutoff had a sensitivity of 77%, near-infrared spectroscopy 85%, and MRI had similar sensitivity, with lower specificity at a given sensitivity [r10]. These findings suggest that raised pressure is part of the picture but that other mechanisms, such as fascial properties, muscle changes and perfusion, may contribute. Unlike acute compartment syndrome, CECS is reversible and does not usually cause necrosis; symptoms settle with rest.

structures.name: Muscle within the affected compartment
structures.effect: Swells with exertion inside a closed compartment; pressure rises and perfusion is compromised [r1]

structures.name: Deep crural fascia
structures.effect: Limits expansion; fascial hernias are found more often in CECS (45.9% versus 12.9%) [r7]

structures.name: Deep peroneal nerve (anterior compartment)
structures.effect: Irritated by raised pressure: paraesthesia and weakness of dorsiflexion [r3]

structures.name: Vessels
structures.effect: Circulation is compromised while pressure is high [r1]

muscles.name: Tibialis anterior, EDL and EHL (anterior)
muscles.effect: Tightness, cramping and weakness of dorsiflexion at a reproducible point in exercise; weakness of dorsiflexion can accompany nerve involvement [r3]

muscles.name: Peroneals (lateral)
muscles.effect: Lateral leg tightness; usually together with anterior symptoms [r5]

muscles.name: Tibialis posterior and long toe flexors (deep posterior)
muscles.effect: Deep medial leg pain overlapping with MTSS [r9]

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius and soleus (superficial posterior)
muscles.effect: Calf tightness, uncommon as a CECS site [r5]

muscles.name: Muscle activation changes
muscles.effect: Data on inhibition, atrophy or altered recruitment in CECS were not found in the sources reviewed; forefoot running shifted load away from the anterior compartment in small series [r1].

cellular.description: Muscle blood flow and volume rise within the compartment; the fascial sleeve limits expansion [r1].
Intramuscular pressure rises and stays elevated after exercise, in many patients above the commonly used thresholds [r7,r4].
Circulation and muscle function are compromised, causing pain and tightness; nerve irritation adds paraesthesia [r1,r3].
Pressure falls and symptoms subside quickly; unlike acute compartment syndrome there is no sustained ischaemia [r2].

systems.effect: Raised pressure compromises circulation during exercise; arterial entrapment syndromes mimic CECS and need exclusion [r1,r9].
Compression of nerves within the compartment causes paraesthesia and weakness; first web space numbness suggests the deep peroneal nerve [r3].
A 6-week program to modify running style (forefoot strike) lowered post-run intracompartmental pressure by 36% and increased running distance by 43% in 19 patients (uncontrolled) [r8].

Reproducible pain limits training and may lead to avoidance; surgical failure was associated with perioperative complications, activity limitations and persistence of pre-operative symptoms (and, in univariate analysis, bilateral involvement) [r6].

timeframes.summary: There is no validated natural history or recovery timeline. In small uncontrolled series, a 6-week program to modify running style produced gains in running distance and symptoms [r8]. After fasciotomy, return depends on the technique and the surgeon's protocol, and results vary. The phases below are typical clinical ranges, not trial-derived timelines.

healing.description: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude look-alikes; reduce provoking volume and keep fitness with non-impact work
Six-week program to modify running style in small series, with symptom-guided progression [r8,r1]
Build run distance and intensity while tracking where symptoms start
If conservative care fails, consider fasciotomy; early rehabilitation follows the surgeon's protocol [r5]

milestones.label: Diagnosis confirmed and look-alikes excluded
milestones.note: Clinical assessment with testing as needed [r9]

milestones.label: 6-week running-style program complete
milestones.note: Small series reported 43% greater running distance and 36% lower post-run intracompartmental pressure [r8]

milestones.label: Surgical decision if conservative care has failed
milestones.note: Typical clinical range after an adequate conservative trial; confirm the diagnosis before surgery [r4]

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based and highly variable. Conservative care allowed symptom-free running after a 6-week running-style program in small series [r8], while fasciotomy is successful in about two-thirds of young athletes, with 27.7% of military patients unable to return to full activity [r5,r6].

symptoms: Pain and tightness in the lower leg that builds at a reproducible time or distance into running or marching, then settles quickly after stopping [r2]
Cramping, a sense of fullness or tightness, and weakness during exercise [r3]
Paraesthesia or numbness in the foot or first web space in anterior compartment CECS [r3]
Symptoms that are absent at rest and in daily walking in the early stages
signs: Usually normal at rest; examine immediately after provocative exercise
Palpable tension or tenderness over the involved compartment after exercise
Muscle herniae through the fascia (45.9% of patients with CECS versus 12.9% of those without) [r7]
Transient sensory loss or weak dorsiflexion immediately after exercise
Normal pulses, no focal bony tenderness and no calf swelling or warmth

subjective: Provocation: the exact time, distance or speed at which symptoms start, and the sport or surface that triggers them
Location: anterior, lateral, deep medial or posterior leg; one or both legs [r2]
Relief: symptoms settling quickly after stopping, rather than lingering for hours [r2]
Neurological features: paraesthesia, numbness or weakness, and whether they resolve fully with rest [r3]
Running style, footwear, training load and previous leg injuries such as MTSS or stress fracture [r9]
Symptoms that suggest alternatives: back pain or leg symptoms with walking (spinal), pain with a cool foot (arterial), or a recent fracture or crush injury (acute compartment syndrome)
observation: Running gait on treadmill or video: foot strike pattern, overstride and cadence [r1]
Visible muscle herniae or bulges in the leg [r7]
palpation: Compartment tension and tenderness, assessed at rest and again within minutes of provocative exercise
Fascial defects or herniae over the anterior and lateral compartments [r7]
Bony tenderness along the tibia, mapped to separate MTSS or stress fracture
rangeOfMotion: Ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion; passive stretch should not reproduce the symptoms at rest
Subtalar and hip range, as contributing factors to running mechanics
strength: Dorsiflexion and great toe extension strength before and immediately after exercise [r3]
neuro: Sensation in the first web space, dorsum of the foot and lateral leg before and after provocation (deep and superficial peroneal nerves) [r3]
Distal pulses at rest and in plantarflexion or dorsiflexion if a vascular cause is possible [r9]
Lumbar screen: slump test, reflexes and back movements when leg pain does not follow a compartment pattern
functional: Provocative treadmill or track run to symptom onset with a pain rating, then immediate re-examination for tension, herniae and neurological change
Single-leg hop and calf raise tests to exclude bone stress injury and measure capacity
Running video analysis for foot strike and cadence [r1]

specialTests.name: Dynamic intracompartmental pressure measurement
specialTests.purpose: Measure compartment pressure before and after provocative exercise
specialTests.procedure: A needle or slit catheter is placed in the compartment under local anaesthesia. Pressure is recorded at rest, after exercise at 1 and 5 minutes, and during relaxation.
specialTests.positive: Pedowitz criteria: pre-exercise 15 mmHg or more, 1-minute post-exercise 30 mmHg or more, or 5-minute post-exercise 20 mmHg or more [r7]. These thresholds overlap the range in healthy subjects, except for relaxation pressure [r4], so interpret in context.

specialTests.name: Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS)
specialTests.purpose: Non-invasive measure of muscle oxygenation during exercise
specialTests.procedure: A sensor is placed over the muscle and oxygenation is recorded during and after exercise on a treadmill.
specialTests.positive: Abnormal oxygenation pattern defined by the study protocol. In a prospective study of 50 patients its sensitivity was clinically equivalent to that of pressure measurement [r10].

specialTests.name: In-scanner exercise MRI
specialTests.purpose: Non-invasive screening for anterior compartment CECS
specialTests.procedure: T2-weighted MRI is acquired before and after in-scanner exercise, and a T2 intensity ratio is calculated for the compartment.
specialTests.positive: A T2 intensity ratio of 1.54 or higher was used as the threshold in the validation study (anterior compartments) [r11].
specialTests.sensitivity: 96% (95% CI 79–99) against the final clinical impression; 87% against needle manometry
specialTests.specificity: 87% (95% CI 75–94) against the final clinical impression; 62% against needle manometry

specialTests.name: Exercise provocation with immediate re-examination
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce symptoms and document the signs at the time
specialTests.procedure: The athlete runs on a treadmill or track to symptom onset. Within minutes, examine compartment tension, sensation, dorsiflexion strength and pulses, then re-check at rest.
specialTests.positive: Symptoms, tension or neurological change at exercise that settle with rest. Accuracy was not found in the sources reviewed; some reviews regard the clinical diagnosis as the reference standard [r3].

clinicalRules.name: Pedowitz intramuscular pressure criteria
clinicalRules.description: In the presence of appropriate clinical findings, one or more of a pre-exercise pressure of 15 mmHg or more, a 1-minute post-exercise pressure of 30 mmHg or more, or a 5-minute post-exercise pressure of 20 mmHg or more is considered diagnostic [r7]. A systematic review found these criteria overlap the healthy range, so protocol-specific upper confidence limits are recommended to guide diagnosis after failed conservative management [r4].

outcomeMeasures.name: Lower Leg Outcome Survey (LLOS)
outcomeMeasures.use: Patient-reported function and symptoms of the lower leg; used in a gait retraining series [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE)
outcomeMeasures.use: Single-item rating of overall leg condition [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient Specific Complaints (PSC)
outcomeMeasures.use: Individual rating of the most limiting activities [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Running distance or time to symptom onset
outcomeMeasures.use: Practical measure of response; running distance rose 43% after a 6-week program in one series [r8]

imaging.indication: Non-invasive screening or when pressure measurement is not available [r11]
imaging.findings: Increased T2 signal ratio in the affected compartment after exercise; sensitivity 96% and specificity 87% in a validation study of anterior compartments [r11]

imaging.indication: Exclude stress fracture, tumour, muscle or fascial tear, and other causes of exercise-induced leg pain [r9]
imaging.findings: Normal in CECS; used to exclude other causes

imaging.indication: Suspected functional popliteal artery entrapment, which can mimic CECS [r9]
imaging.findings: Arterial compression with plantarflexion or dorsiflexion

imaging.indication: Emerging tools mentioned in reviews; not yet established [r3]
imaging.findings: Increased muscle stiffness; diagnostic accuracy was not found in the sources reviewed

differentials.name: Medial tibial stress syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Diffuse tenderness along the posteromedial tibial border; deep posterior CECS overlaps with MTSS and the two can coexist [r9].

differentials.name: Tibial stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Focal bony tenderness, pain on hopping, and pain that lingers after stopping [r9].

differentials.name: Functional popliteal artery entrapment
differentials.distinguishing: Claudication-like calf pain that eases quickly with rest, with possible pulse loss on plantarflexion or dorsiflexion; MR angiography is the primary investigation [r9].

differentials.name: Nerve entrapment (common or superficial peroneal)
differentials.distinguishing: Burning or numbness in a nerve distribution, often with a local tender point or entrapment site; conservative treatment is preferred [r9].

differentials.name: Lumbar radicular pain or spinal stenosis
differentials.distinguishing: Back involvement, neurological signs, symptoms with walking and relief with flexion or sitting rather than at a set exercise intensity. Spinal pathologies are a recognised differential for exercise-related leg pain [r2].

differentials.name: Calf muscle strain
differentials.distinguishing: Clear onset during activity, local muscle tenderness and pain with resisted contraction or stretch rather than a reproducible exercise threshold.

differentials.name: Acute compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Acute onset after fracture, crush or direct injury with tense swelling, escalating pain on passive stretch and no relief with rest. This is an emergency [r12].

redFlags: Severe, escalating leg pain with a tense swollen compartment, pain on passive stretch of the toes or new paraesthesia, particularly after fracture, direct blow or crush: acute compartment syndrome. Surgical emergency; send to the emergency department immediately [r12].
Claudication-like pain, a cool or pale foot, or reduced pulses on exertion: refer for vascular assessment for popliteal artery entrapment [r9].
Weakness or foot drop that does not recover within minutes of stopping: urgent neurological or vascular review.
Focal bony tenderness, night pain or pain at rest: stress fracture work-up with MRI before further running [r9].
Dark urine, severe muscle swelling and pain after very hard exertion: exertional rhabdomyolysis; urgent medical assessment.
Unilateral calf swelling, warmth and tenderness: same-day assessment for deep vein thrombosis.

management.principles: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude look-alikes first, because the pressure criteria overlap the healthy range and the diagnosis is often delayed [r4,r2]. Conservative options include activity modification, gait retraining, compression, dry needling and botulinum toxin injections, with fasciotomy for persistent symptoms [r2,r3]. Evidence for conservative care is limited to small uncontrolled series [r1,r8]. Surgery is effective in many but not all patients: success was about two-thirds in young athletes, and in 611 military patients 44.7% reported recurrent symptoms and 27.7% could not return to full activity [r5,r6]. Counsel realistically and share the decision.

medical.name: Diagnostic testing (dynamic intracompartmental pressure, NIRS or exercise MRI)
medical.description: Confirm the diagnosis before invasive treatment. Dynamic pressure testing with provocative exercise is often regarded as the reference test, but its criteria overlap healthy values; use protocol-specific upper limits after failed conservative management [r9,r4]. NIRS and MRI have comparable sensitivity [r10,r11].

medical.name: Fasciotomy (open or endoscopically assisted)
medical.description: Release of the involved compartments after failed conservative care. In 24 studies (1,596 patients) the operation was successful in about two-thirds of young athletic patients, 84% were satisfied, 6% needed revision and the complication rate was 13% [r5]. In 611 military patients, 44.7% had symptom recurrence, 15.7% had complications and 17.3% were referred for medical discharge [r6]. Surgery provides the best outcome in some reviews, but evidence is observational [r9].

medical.name: Botulinum toxin injection
medical.description: Injection of the involved muscle is described as a conservative option in recent reviews [r3,r2]. Controlled trials were not identified in the sources reviewed.

physio.name: Gait retraining to a forefoot or midfoot strike
physio.description: A 6-week program to modify running style: in two cases, intracompartmental pressure fell and running distance and speed rose without symptoms [r1]. In 19 patients, post-run pressure fell 36% and running distance rose 43%; home-based training did not differ significantly from centre-based training [r8]. Uncontrolled, small studies.

physio.name: Activity modification and cross-training
physio.description: Reduce the exercise that provokes symptoms and keep fitness with cycling or swimming [r2].

physio.name: Soft-tissue therapy, dry needling and compression stockings
physio.description: Listed among conservative options [r2]. No trials in CECS were identified in the sources reviewed.

physio.name: Strength and capacity work for the lower limb
physio.description: General leg, hip and trunk strengthening to optimise running biomechanics, as part of gait retraining [r8].

physio.name: Education and expectation setting
physio.description: Explain that raised pressure is a recognised mechanism, that symptoms are reproducible and not dangerous, and that surgery has meaningful failure rates [r6].

education: CECS is a pressure problem inside the leg compartments during exercise. It is not a muscle tear or a fracture, and the symptoms settle with rest.
A trial of changing how you run (landing nearer the middle or front of the foot) helped some people in small studies, and it is worth trying before surgery.
Surgery works well for many people, but not everyone; about one in four or more may not return to full activity, so confirm the diagnosis first.
Stop if you get severe, constant pain, a hard swollen leg or numbness that does not settle; that is an emergency.
Keep fit with cycling or swimming while you work on your running.

rehab.overview: Progression is symptom-guided: confirm the diagnosis, modify load and fitness, then run a structured gait retraining program, then rebuild running with close tracking of where symptoms start. The gait program in the published series lasted 6 weeks [r8]. After fasciotomy, follow the surgeon's protocol; the stages below suit both non-operative and post-operative care once wounds have healed. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not trial-derived. As working rules, keep exercise symptoms at 3/10 or less and settled quickly after stopping (clinical convention).

stages.name: Confirm and modify load
goals: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude look-alikes
Reduce provoking volume without losing fitness
Baseline measures of symptom onset and LLOS
precautions: Refer if any red flag is present
Do not run through severe pain or numbness
After surgery, no impact until wounds are healed and the surgeon clears loading

exercises.name: Cycling or swimming
exercises.dosage: 30–45 min, 3–5 days a week at an effort that stays below symptom onset
exercises.cues: Maintain fitness without the repeated foot strike

exercises.name: Ankle range of motion (seated)
exercises.cues: Move smoothly through the full range

progressionCriteria: Diagnosis confirmed or alternative diagnoses excluded
Baseline running tolerance recorded (time to symptom onset)

stages.name: Gait retraining
goals: Change to a midfoot or forefoot strike
Raise step rate and shorten stride
Build calf and foot capacity to cope with the new pattern
precautions: Increase forefoot loading gradually to protect the calf and Achilles
Stop if calf pain or new symptoms appear

exercises.name: Forefoot strike drills (walking and short jogs)
exercises.dosage: 10–15 min, 3–4 days a week, with video or mirror feedback [r1]
exercises.cues: Land under the hips on the ball of the foot, heel kissing the ground

exercises.name: Step-rate cueing
exercises.dosage: Raise cadence by about 5–10% with a metronome during drills [r8]

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–15, 3 s up and 3 s down, 3 days a week

progressionCriteria: Consistent forefoot or midfoot landing at drill pace
Calf raise endurance sufficient for the new pattern, with no calf pain

stages.name: Graded running with symptom monitoring
goals: Build run time and distance below symptom onset
Maintain the new running style at fatigue
precautions: Do not push through exercise-limiting tightness or numbness
Hold the load if symptoms return earlier than the previous run

exercises.name: Walk–run or short interval runs
exercises.dosage: Alternate days, starting at about 60–70% of the symptom-free time and extending by about 10% a week
exercises.cues: Stop before symptoms begin to build

exercises.name: Cadence-controlled easy runs
exercises.cues: Hold the step rate when tired

progressionCriteria: Symptom-free 30 min of continuous running on two consecutive runs
Symptom threshold moved beyond the pre-treatment baseline

stages.name: Return to sport and maintenance
goals: Return to usual training and sport demands
Retain gait changes under fatigue and at speed
Decide on surgical referral if symptoms persist
precautions: If symptoms persist despite an adequate trial, repeat assessment and consider surgical referral after confirming the diagnosis [r4]
After fasciotomy, progress to impact only as the surgeon allows

exercises.name: Progressive run volume then intensity
exercises.dosage: Build distance first, then hills and intervals over several weeks

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills
exercises.dosage: Cutting, accelerations and sport drills added in steps

exercises.name: Gait refreshers
exercises.dosage: Weekly short sessions with video feedback
exercises.cues: Check landing and cadence when tired

progressionCriteria: Full training week without exercise-limiting symptoms
LLOS and SANE improved from baseline [r8]

criteria: Symptom-free running at the distance and intensity required by the sport on at least two or three consecutive sessions (clinical convention)
No tightness, numbness or weakness during or after exercise [r3]
Symmetrical calf raise endurance and single-leg hop (about 90%, clinical convention)
After fasciotomy: wounds healed, surgeon clearance and graded loading [r5]
tests: Graded running test with symptom-onset timing
Post-exercise examination of tension and sensation
Single-leg hop and calf raise endurance

prognosis: Conservative care has only small uncontrolled series behind it. In 19 patients a 6-week running-style program lowered post-run intracompartmental pressure by 36% and increased running distance by 43%, with continued improvement in self-reported scores at 4 months [r8]. After surgery, about two-thirds of young athletic patients had a successful result and 84% were satisfied, with a 6% revision rate and a 13% complication rate [r5]. In 611 military patients, 44.7% reported symptom recurrence, 27.7% were unable to return to full activity, 5.9% needed revision and 17.3% were referred for medical discharge; failure was associated with perioperative complications, activity limitations and persistence of pre-operative symptoms (and, in univariate analysis, bilateral involvement) [r6]. Long-term outcomes of conservative care were not found in the sources reviewed.
prevention: No strategy to prevent CECS has been tested in the sources reviewed.
Changing to a forefoot or midfoot strike reduced symptoms in small series, but it has not been tested as prevention [r8,r1].
Early recognition of reproducible exertional leg pain shortens the delay to diagnosis, which is a recognised problem [r2].
clinicalPearls: Pain that begins at a reproducible point in exercise and settles quickly after stopping points to CECS rather than bone stress injury [r2,r9].
Examine immediately after provocation. Compartment tension, herniae and neurological change are often absent at rest [r7].
Do not rely on a single pressure value: the criteria overlap the healthy range, so use protocol-specific limits, NIRS or MRI as supporting information [r4,r10,r11].
Deep posterior CECS overlaps with MTSS and the two can coexist, so assess for both [r9].
Set honest expectations about surgery: about two-thirds of young athletes succeed, and nearly one in four military patients could not return to full activity [r5,r6].
Try gait retraining before surgery, but acknowledge that the evidence is from small, uncontrolled series [r8].

animation.title: How chronic exertional compartment syndrome develops

captions.text: A runner sets off at a normal training pace.
The leg muscles work with every stride.
As the run goes on, blood flow to the muscles and their volume rise.
Tightness and pain build in the shin at a predictable point in the run.
Zooming into the right shin, viewed from the front.
The anterior compartment holds tibialis anterior, EDL, EHL, the deep peroneal nerve and an artery.
With running, the muscles work hard and swell inside a space bounded by bone and fascia.
Pressure rises because the fascia cannot expand.
Circulation is compromised and the nerve is irritated: pain, tightness and paraesthesia.
Symptoms build at a predictable point in the run.
On stopping, pressure falls and symptoms settle within minutes.
If conservative care fails, fasciotomy releases the compartment.
Resting compartment: muscle fibres and capillaries sit inside a tight fascial sleeve.
With exercise, muscle blood flow and volume rise and the compartment swells.
Pressure rises because the fascia cannot stretch.
Higher pressure impairs venous outflow and perfusion, a proposed cause of pain and tightness.
On stopping, or after fasciotomy, pressure falls and circulation recovers.
